captures.notes: Verified by program: record.length 108 == actual 108; handshake.length 104 == actual 104; extensions.length 32 == actual 32. Chosen values: random, session_id. Critical decoding subtlety: the client offered status_request (0x0005) and supported_groups/signature_algorithms; the server echoed NONE of them. The ABSENCE of 0x0005 is the OCSP-stapling refusal — negative information carried by a field that is not on the wire. No flat-capture decoder can represent "this extension was declined" as distinct from "the decoder did not look". Also note this record deliberately carries ONE handshake message; a real server usually coalesces ServerHello+Certificate+ServerKeyExchange+ServerHelloDone into one or more records with no alignment between record boundaries and message boundaries.

statefulness:
TLS is close to a worst case for §5, and it breaks the state model in ways the "known gaps" list only half anticipates.

LEGAL-MESSAGE-PER-STATE. States are: tcpConnected -> clientHelloSent -> serverHelloReceived -> serverFlightComplete -> keysExchanged -> clientCcsSent (client write half now ENCRYPTED) -> serverCcsReceived (read half ENCRYPTED) -> established -> closed. ClientHello is validIn tcpConnected (and, for renegotiation, established — a genuinely different meaning in the same wire form, distinguished only by a non-empty renegotiation_info). Everything after ServerHello is validIn exactly one state. `validIn` handles this fine.

MANDATED CHAINING IS FLIGHT-SHAPED, NOT MESSAGE-SHAPED, and v0 has no flight primitive. The server's reply is an ORDERED sequence — ServerHello, Certificate, [ServerKeyExchange], [CertificateRequest], ServerHelloDone — where some members are optional *as a function of the cipher suite selected two messages earlier* (ECDHE mandates ServerKeyExchange; static RSA forbids it). `requires:["serverHello"]` cannot express "these five, in this order, with membership determined by a field in the first one". Worse, the flight has NO relationship to record boundaries: all five may arrive in one record, or ServerHello may be split across two. `frame` is declared once per connection and there is only one level of it, so the record framer and the handshake-message framer cannot coexist.

MUTUAL EXCLUSION. `conflicts` is per-session and symmetric; TLS needs directional exclusion keyed on negotiation. If the server selects a static-RSA suite, ServerKeyExchange must NEVER appear; if it selects ECDHE, it must ALWAYS appear. That is not "never in the same session", it is "forbidden given a value decoded earlier". Similarly, once ChangeCipherSpec is sent, no further plaintext handshake message may be emitted in that direction — a state that forbids a wire ENCODING, not a message.

NEGOTIATED CAPABILITY — the spec flags this as a known gap and TLS confirms it as blocking, in three distinct flavours the gap note conflates. (i) Narrowing selection: client offers 8 cipher suites, server returns 1, and it MUST be a member of the offered set — an unoffered suite is a protocol violation the grammar cannot detect. (ii) Same for ALPN: 2 offered, 1 returned. (iii) ABSENCE AS DECLINE: my client offered status_request (0x0005); the server's reply contains no 0x0005, and that silence IS the OCSP refusal. Likewise extended_master_secret present in both = agreed, present in one = not agreed. The model needs "the response's extension SET is the negotiation result, and a missing member is a negative fact", which no per-field capture expresses. Note the direction of the risk: a flat-capture decoder reports the same nothing for "declined" and "I didn't parse it".

PRESUMED VS CONFIRMED. Everything about the connection is presumed until the Finished exchange. Between ServerHello and Finished the client presumes the cipher suite, the version, the peer identity and the transcript; the peer's Finished — a MAC over the whole handshake transcript — is the single confirmation for all of it. So TLS has one deferred bulk confirmation, not per-message `confirmedBy`. `confirmedBy: {message, matches}` is per-message and compares captures; it cannot say "message N confirms messages 1..N-1 via a cryptographic accumulator". And that accumulator needs the RAW BYTES of every received handshake message, which decode never exposes.

DISCOVERING STATE IS WRONG FROM THE NEXT RESPONSE — pervasive here, and the `implies` hook is the right shape but too weak. Cases: (a) the reply is an Alert record (0x15) not a Handshake record, e.g. 15 03 03 00 02 02 28 = fatal handshake_failure, meaning no common suite; selecting the parse by contentType needs a switch. (b) The server echoes the client's session_id => resumption, so the expected next flight is CCS+Finished, not Certificate — a WHOLE DIFFERENT flight selected by comparing a decoded field against a value we sent. (c) A resumption we believed valid is refused by a fresh session_id, and we only learn it one message later. (d) After CCS, a decryption failure surfaces as bad_record_mac — the "session is wrong" signal arrives as an opaque encrypted-layer error, not a status field. `implies` can key on capture.status; it cannot key on "the transform failed".

SEQUENCE NUMBERS. The record layer carries an implicit 64-bit per-direction sequence number that is NEVER on the wire but is fed into every MAC/AEAD nonce, and it RESETS TO ZERO on each ChangeCipherSpec (epoch change). `seq.next` is a single persisted monotonic counter — wrong cardinality (needs per-direction), wrong lifetime (needs reset-on-event), and it is invisible-yet-load-bearing, which no field can be in v0.

FRAGMENTATION/REASSEMBLY. Two independent axes: a handshake message spanning records (reassembly upward) and multiple handshake messages inside one record (demultiplexing downward). Both must work simultaneously, and a Certificate message routinely exceeds one 16 KiB record. The single `frame` declaration cannot express a two-level framer.

RETRANSMIT/DEDUP. Not applicable over TCP — this is the one listed gap TLS does not exercise. (DTLS would.)

MODAL/EXCLUSIVE STATE — applies in an unlisted form: after CCS the connection is in a mode where the WIRE ENCODING itself changes. The same `parse` document is no longer valid for any subsequent record; bodies become AEAD ciphertext. The state model governs which messages are legal but has no concept of a state that rebinds the codec.

gaps.what: No byte-budgeted iteration. `each` takes an item COUNT; a list of variable-width items inside a known byte span cannot be decoded. This kills the entire extensions block — 98 of 196 bytes in the ClientHello, 32 of 113 in the ServerHello.
gaps.why: At CH offset 96 the field extensions.length = 0x0062 (98). The 98 bytes that follow are 9 extensions of widths 20, 6, 14, 18, 4, 5, 4, 9, 18. Correct decode is `while consumed < 98 { type=u16be; len=u16be; skip len }`. There is no expression yielding 9 from 98 — the count is only discoverable by walking. `{"each":"98/…"}` has no divisor. `{"each":"9"}` is a lie that breaks the moment an extension is added, and cannot be derived from the bytes.
gaps.proposedFix:
Let `each` take a byte budget as an alternative to a count, and fail if the walk does not land exactly on the boundary:
{ "each": { "overBytes": "capture.extensionsLen" }, "as": "extensions",
  "fields": [ {"u16be":null,"as":"type"}, {"u16be":null,"as":"length"}, {"bytes":"item.length","as":"body"} ],
  "onOverrun": "error", "onUnderrun": "error" }
In encode mode the same field emits the items and the budget is back-patched by the enclosing len(group:). This one primitive is the single highest-value fix in the whole report.

gaps.what: No Record kind in ProtoValue and no per-iteration capture scope, so a list of structured items cannot be represented even if it could be walked.
gaps.why: Each of the 9 extensions is a triple {type, length, body}. ProtoValue is `Bytes | Int | Text | List`. `{"each":…,"as":"registers"}` yields a flat List of scalars. There is no way to express capture.extensions[3].type == 0x000d, and `as:` on a field inside an `each` has no defined per-iteration binding — the second iteration would overwrite the first.
gaps.proposedFix: Add `Record` to ProtoValue (`Bytes | Int | Text | List | Record`) and define `item.*` as the current-iteration scope inside `each`. Inner `as:` names become record members; the outer `as:` yields List<Record>. Indexing and member access in expressions: `capture.extensions[i].type`, `capture.extensions | find(.type == 0x0010) | .body`. This is the only fix in the report that genuinely requires an engine change, and gaps 1, 4 and 11 all depend on it.

gaps.what: No fixed- or variable-width raw byte capture in decode mode. Fields that are semantically opaque byte strings decode to List<Int> or not at all.
gaps.why: CH offset 11 is a 32-byte random; offset 44 is a 32-byte session_id. `value` needs an expression (none exists in decode), `skip` discards, `repeat` is only defined on encode-side `value`. The only surviving option, `{"each":"32","fields":[{"u8":null}],"as":"random"}`, produces List<Int> — not ProtoValue.Bytes — so `capture.random | hex` is a validate-time type error and the value cannot be fed back into an encode document. Round-trip is broken at offset 11, before the hard part.

gaps.what: No dispatch on a just-decoded tag. Needed at two levels: record content_type, and extension_type.
gaps.why: CH byte 0 is 0x16; the same connection legally carries 0x14 ChangeCipherSpec, 0x15 Alert (a fatal reply is `15 03 03 00 02 02 28`), 0x17 ApplicationData — each with a completely different body layout. Inside the extensions block, type 0x0000 has body {u16 list_len, u8 name_type, u16 host_len, host} while type 0x0010 has {u16 list_len, then n×(u8 len, bytes)} and 0x0017 has an empty body. `when:` can only include or exclude one field; it cannot select among alternative field LISTS, and inside an iteration it has nothing to test against.
gaps.proposedFix:
{ "switch": "item.type",
  "cases": { "0x0000": [ {"u16be":null,"as":"listLen"}, {"u8":null,"as":"nameType"}, {"u16be":null,"as":"hostLen"}, {"bytes":"item.hostLen","as":"host"} ],
              "0x0010": [ {"u16be":null,"as":"listLen"}, {"each":{"overBytes":"item.listLen"},"as":"protocols","fields":[ {"u8":null,"as":"n"}, {"bytes":"item.n","as":"name"} ]} ] },
  "default": [ { "bytes": "item.length", "as": "raw" } ] }
The `default` arm is what makes forward compatibility expressible: unknown extensions are preserved as opaque bytes rather than aborting the parse. Symmetric in encode mode, which also fixes data-driven extension ordering (gap 11).

gaps.what: No `remaining()` / `offset()` expression, so an optional trailing region is undecidable and truncation is undetectable.
gaps.why: A ClientHello may legally END after compression_methods, with no extensions_length field at all (SSLv3-era clients, and TLS 1.0/1.1 clients in the wild). Whether byte 96 is `extensions.length` or past-the-end is decided by comparing bytes consumed so far against handshake.length = 187 — decoder position state that no v0 expression exposes. The identical predicate governs every optional TLS extension body.

gaps.what: No length-prefixed vector primitive. TLS's universal building block is `vector<T>` — a length prefix followed by homogeneous items with NO type tag — and `tlvList` mandates a `t`.
gaps.why: Six vectors appear in the ClientHello alone: cipher_suites (u16 prefix, 2-byte items), compression_methods (u8, 1-byte), extensions (u16, variable), server_name_list (u16, variable), supported_groups (u16, 2-byte), ALPN protocol_name_list (u16, variable with u8 sub-prefixes). None has a type tag, so `tlvList` is unusable for every one of them. Today each needs a hand-written group + len(group:) pair in encode and is undecodable in decode.
gaps.proposedFix:
{ "vector": { "l": "u16be", "of": { "fields": [ {"u16be":null} ] }, "items": "inputs.cipherSuites", "as": "cipherSuites" } }
The length is derived on encode and consumed as the iteration budget on decode — one declaration, both directions, no back-patch group needed. Generalise `tlvList` as the special case where `of` begins with a tag field. This collapses all three nesting levels of the nominated hazard into one construct and is the second-highest-value fix after `overBytes`.

gaps.what: `len(group:X)` inside an `each` is undefined — group names have no per-iteration scope.
gaps.why: ALPN needs, per item, a u8 length covering that item's bytes. I could only encode it as `{"u8":"p | ascii | len"}` — deriving the length from the VALUE rather than from a span. That works for a string but fails for any item whose length is not computable from its own value: a nested group, a conditional sub-field, an item containing its own sub-vector. In a TLS Certificate message (`vector<vector<opaque>>`, each cert with its own u24 length) this is fatal, and it is the same shape as the ALPN case.

gaps.what: Only one `frame` per connection, but TLS framing is two-level and the levels are not aligned.
gaps.why: Record framing is {u8 type, u16 version, u16 length} — a length prefix at offset 3, not the spec's example offset 4. Handshake-message framing is {u8 type, u24 length} INSIDE the reassembled record stream. A Certificate message routinely exceeds one record and must be reassembled across records; conversely ServerHello+Certificate+ServerKeyExchange+ServerHelloDone are routinely coalesced into one record. Message boundaries and record boundaries are independent. A single `frame` declaration cannot express both, and no v0 construct spans records.
gaps.proposedFix:
Give a stream layer a framer chain, with the inner framer applied to the concatenated payload of same-type records:
{ "kind":"tls",
  "frame": { "kind":"lengthPrefixed", "prefix":"u16be", "at":3, "includesPrefix":false, "demuxBy":{"at":0,"width":"u8","as":"contentType"} },
  "inner": { "when":"contentType == 0x16", "frame":{ "kind":"lengthPrefixed", "prefix":"u24be", "at":1, "includesPrefix":false } } }
The engine concatenates payloads per demux key and re-frames. This also covers the general "records carry a substream" case (BACnet segmentation, WebSocket continuation).

gaps.what: No state-bound wire transform. After ChangeCipherSpec the record body becomes AEAD ciphertext and the parse document silently stops applying.
gaps.why: Record 3 of the handshake is `14 03 03 00 01 01` (ChangeCipherSpec). Every record after it in that direction has an encrypted body: with AES-128-GCM, {8-byte explicit nonce || ciphertext || 16-byte tag}, whose plaintext is only then a handshake message. §5 governs which MESSAGES are legal in a state; it has no concept of a state that rebinds the CODEC. There is no v0 document that can read a full TLS session.
gaps.proposedFix:
"states": { "encrypted": { "transform": { "decode":"aead.open", "encode":"aead.seal",
    "keys":"session.keys", "aad":"session.recordSeq | be(8) | concat(field:contentType, field:version, field:length)" } } },
"transitions": [ { "from":"handshaking", "to":"encrypted", "on":"changeCipherSpec", "perDirection":true } ]
The transform sits between the framer and the field decoder, so the SAME parse block applies to the plaintext. `perDirection` matters: the two halves switch independently.

gaps.what: No cross-message accumulator and no raw-span capture, so the handshake transcript hash is impossible — which means the single confirmation point of the whole protocol cannot be modelled.
gaps.why: Finished carries verify_data = PRF(master_secret, label, SHA256(all handshake messages, headers included, from ClientHello onward)). That is a digest over the concatenated RAW BYTES of every message in both directions. `checksum` spans are intra-message (`from:start to:here`); `msg.<name>` gives bytes of messages WE encoded, never of messages we received; decode exposes named captures but never the underlying bytes. Without this the client cannot verify the server, and every presumed fact about the session stays permanently unconfirmed.
gaps.proposedFix:
Two parts. (i) Expose the raw span in decode: { "capture":"raw", "as":"msgBytes", "over":"group:handshake" }. (ii) Declare a session-scoped accumulator fed by message events:
"accumulators": { "transcript": { "scope":"session", "alg":"sha256", "feed":"raw",
  "include":["clientHello","serverHello","certificate","serverKeyExchange","serverHelloDone","clientKeyExchange"], "ordered":true } }
readable as `session.transcript.digest`. This generalises to any protocol with a running MAC over a message history (SSH exchange hash, Noise, SRTP).

gaps.what: No modelling of narrowing negotiation or of absence-as-decline.
gaps.why: Three instances in one 113-byte response. (i) The client offered 8 cipher suites; the server returned exactly one, 0xc02f, which MUST be a member of the offered set — an unoffered value is a protocol violation nothing detects. (ii) ALPN: 2 offered, "h2" returned. (iii) The client offered status_request (0x0005) and the server's extension list does NOT contain it — that silence IS the OCSP-stapling refusal. Negative information carried by a field that is not on the wire cannot be captured by any per-field construct, and a flat-capture decoder renders "declined" identically to "not parsed".
gaps.proposedFix:
"negotiates": [
  { "offered":"inputs.cipherSuites", "selected":"capture.cipherSuite", "mustBeMemberOf":true,
    "onViolation":"fail", "as":"session.cipherSuite" },
  { "offered":"inputs.alpn", "selected":"capture.extensions | find(.type==0x0010) | .body",
    "absentMeans":"declined", "as":"session.alpn" },
  { "offered":"'status_request'", "present":"capture.extensions | any(.type==0x0005)",
    "absentMeans":"declined", "as":"session.ocspStapling" } ]
Each entry emits a fact with confidence "confirmed" (the peer said so) or an explicit declined fact. Directly answers the spec's own open question about MQTT SUBACK.

gaps.what: No consistency assertion between nested length fields, and no bounded sub-parse.
gaps.why: Nothing in the parse block may state hsLength == recordLength - 4 (187 == 191-4), or that the extension walk lands exactly on extensionsLen. I verified all three levels with an external script; the grammar cannot. A record declaring recordLength 191 but carrying hsLength 999 decodes 'successfully' into garbage, and the error surfaces far downstream.
gaps.proposedFix:
{ "assert": "capture.hsLength == capture.recordLength - 4", "onFail": "error", "message": "handshake length disagrees with record length" }
Plus an `extent` on decode-mode groups (see gap 5) so the engine checks the closure automatically: a group whose fields consume more or fewer bytes than its declared extent is a decode error, not silent drift.

gaps.what: No width constraint on an encode-mode `value`, so a wrong-sized input yields a wrong packet with all three length fields self-consistently wrong.
gaps.why: `{"value":"inputs.clientRandom | unhex"}` emits whatever it is given. A 31-byte random produces a 195-byte record with recordLength 190 and hsLength 186 — internally consistent, structurally valid, cryptographically dead. Nothing at validate or encode time catches it. The two-pass back-patcher actively hides the bug by making the lengths agree.
gaps.proposedFix:
{ "value":"inputs.clientRandom | unhex", "size":32, "onSizeMismatch":"error" }
with `size` also accepting an expression. Combined with the decode-mode `bytes` field (gap 3) this gives one width-checked byte-string construct in both directions.

gaps.what: Extension order is document structure, not data — so encode(decode(bytes)) cannot reproduce an arbitrary observed ordering.
gaps.why: My encode document fixes the order 0000, 000b, 000a, 000d, 0023, ff01, 0017, 0005, 0010. A different client emits the same nine extensions in a different order; the bytes differ, and the ordering is itself the identity signal (JA3/JA4 fingerprinting). Even given a working decoder, replaying a captured ClientHello byte-for-byte is impossible without editing the JSON. This is a genuine canonical-form ambiguity: TLS permits any extension order, so 'the canonical encoding' does not exist, and the grammar has no way to say 'preserve what you saw'.
gaps.proposedFix:
Allow `switch` in encode mode, driven by a list input, so ordering becomes data:
{ "each":"inputs.extensionOrder", "as":"e",
  "switch":"e", "cases": { "server_name":[ … ], "alpn":[ … ] } }
and let a decoded List<Record> round-trip directly: { "each":"capture.extensions", "as":"e", "fields":[ {"u16be":"e.type"}, {"u16be":"e.body | len"}, {"value":"e.body"} ] } — which makes byte-exact replay of unknown extensions fall out of the opaque `default` arm in gap 4.

gaps.what: No per-direction, event-reset sequence counter. `seq.next` is a single persisted monotonic.
gaps.why: The TLS record layer maintains a 64-bit sequence number per direction that never appears on the wire but is an input to every MAC and AEAD nonce, and it RESETS TO ZERO at each ChangeCipherSpec. `seq.*` has the wrong cardinality (one, not two), the wrong lifetime (persisted per device, not per epoch), and no reset trigger. An invisible-but-load-bearing value has no representation in v0 at all.
gaps.proposedFix:
"counters": { "recordSeq": { "scope":"session", "perDirection":true, "width":"u64", "start":0, "resetOn":"changeCipherSpec", "advanceOn":"record" } }
referenced as `counters.recordSeq` in the transform's aad expression (gap 9). Generalises to DTLS epochs, ZigBee/Z-Wave frame counters and any replay-protected link.

gaps.what: No masked-value / ignore rule for GREASE.
gaps.why: RFC 8701 clients insert reserved values of the form 0x?a?a (0x0a0a, 0x1a1a, … 0xfafa) into the cipher_suites, supported_groups and extensions lists, which peers must ignore. A decoder that treats extension type 0x3a3a as unknown-but-real will mis-fingerprint, and an encoder replaying a capture must reproduce them in place.

gaps.what: `checksum` over `from:start to:here` is ambiguous once spans nest three deep.
gaps.why: With record > handshake > chBody > exts > sniData > sniList, `start` could reasonably mean the message start, the enclosing group's start, or the innermost group's start. TLS 1.2 ClientHello has no checksum so nothing breaks here, but the same three-level nesting exists in protocols that do (BACnet, DNP3), and the ambiguity is latent in every document that nests.
